name: Karl Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a family-owned supermarket in my hometown, part of a small chain of six stores run by the same family for three generations. I'm on the tills most days and I do the Saturday morning fruit and veg delivery check. I like that the owner still walks the floor and knows my name. What wears me out is the new card machines that freeze when it's busy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's home life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine years, since school, and they pay me well for a till job because I've been loyal. I live with my fiancée Elena, and we're getting married next summer at the church we both grew up in. My dad taught me to save, so I've got a good year of pay put by and my car's paid off. I don't touch AI, I don't trust it and I don't need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it was all talk from the big tech firms. At work we'd have a laugh about it at break. I'm not online much, so that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life goes on, which is what I want. The family that owns the store won't rush to replace us. My worries are the wedding bill and getting a house, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts, keep saving for the wedding and a house deposit. We'd go ahead with the church wedding next summer. Nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wedding cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About twelve thousand all in, and we're paying half each with help from both families. It's a lot, but we planned for it. After that, the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI for anything, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Elena uses it for wedding lists, that's her business. I'll stick to pen and paper.

say: I'd say it was all **talk** from the big tech firms.
I'd **laugh about it** at break with colleagues, not online.
think: Life goes on, and the **family owners** won't rush to replace us.
My worries are the **wedding bill** and getting a house, not computers.
do: Keep my shifts and save for the **wedding** and a house deposit.
Go ahead with the **church wedding** next summer as planned.
S0.quote: The family that owns the store won't rush to replace us.
fieldNote: He trusts the **family owners** more than he'd trust a big chain.
His pressures are the **wedding** and a house, both planned for.

steps.text: Keep working the tills at the family-owned supermarket
Hold the church wedding with Elena next summer
Save for a house deposit after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big companies are pushing this to save money, not to help anyone. At work I'd say our owners are different. At church I'd say hard work still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deep down, I'd worry about the bigger chains near us. If they cut prices with robots, our owner might have to follow. The thinking stuff is office work, so not me, but the slow robots would get to us eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save a bit more, maybe two hundred extra a month. I'd wait and see what the owner does before changing anything. I'd still get married next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any of the new tools to stay safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. If the owner says we have to, I'll do it, but I won't go looking. I don't see why I should change for something I didn't ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the store started cutting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big chains and the tech companies, for starting the race. Not our owner. Our owner would be doing it to survive.

say: I'd say **big companies** push this to save money, not to help anyone.
At church I'd say **hard work** still matters.
think: The **bigger chains** cutting prices with robots could force our owner to follow.
The **thinking work** is office stuff, but slow robots would reach us eventually.
do: Keep working and save **£200 extra** a month.
**Wait** for what the owner does and still marry next summer.
S1.quote: I don't see why I should change for something I didn't ask for.
fieldNote: He blames **big chains and tech**, never the family owners.
He'll only learn new tools if the **owner** tells him to.
His **wedding** stays fixed as a sign of stability.

steps.text: Keep working the tills as normal
Save 200 extra a month on top of wedding savings
Wait for the owner's decisions before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and the government should slow it down. I'd say it at church and at the pub. I'd sign anything that put the brakes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is finished by 2031. Even our owner couldn't keep human cashiers if every other shop has robots. The 2028 part wouldn't change my day, but I'd know what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding down, maybe a smaller do at the church hall, and keep the money. I'd talk to my dad about working with him, he's a roofer. I'd keep everything I've saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. It'd keep me up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Elena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Elena we still get married, but small. Then we sit down with my dad and her parents and plan. Family first, that's how we'd get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Roofing gets robots too, eventually. Did you think of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I did, yes. But roofs are high up and old, and every one's different. Maybe it's a few extra years, I don't know.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** and the government should slow it down.
I'd sign anything that put the **brakes** on, at church and at the pub.
think: My job is **finished by 2031** once every shop has robots.
Even our **owner** couldn't keep human cashiers against robot competitors.
do: Cut the wedding to a **smaller do** at the church hall and keep the money.
Talk to my dad about joining his **roofing** work.
feel: **Scared**, kept up at night by it.
S2.quote: Even our owner couldn't keep human cashiers if every other shop has robots.
fieldNote: Fast AGI breaks his trust that the **family owners** can protect him.
He turns to **family**: his dad's roofing and both sets of parents.
He admits roofing only buys **a few years**.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to a small do at the church hall
Sit down with both families to plan finances
Ask his dad about joining the roofing business
Sign petitions asking the government to slow robots down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need time, and five years is better than two. I'd still say it should be slowed down. At work I'd say keep your heads down and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have until 2034 on the tills. That's long enough to learn roofing properly with my dad. I wouldn't like it, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding as planned next summer. I'd start helping my dad on Saturdays from next year, then go full-time around 2030. I'd save hard in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid change. How would it feel to switch trades?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. I've done one thing since school. But my dad did roofing his whole life, so it's still family work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about the store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owner knowing my name, and the old regulars. A roof doesn't say good morning, but roofing pays.

say: I'd say **five years** is better than two, but it should still slow down.
I'd tell colleagues to **keep their heads down** and save.
think: I'd have until about **2034** on the tills, seven more years.
That's long enough to learn **roofing** properly with my dad.
do: Help my dad on **Saturdays** from next year, then go full-time around 2030.
Keep the **wedding** next summer and save hard in between.
S3.quote: A roof doesn't say good morning, but roofing pays.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **switch to family work** without a crash.
He'd miss the **regulars** and the owner knowing his name.
Change is hard for him, but **family** makes it bearable.

steps.text: Help his dad on roofing jobs every Saturday from next year
Hold the church wedding next summer as planned
Save hard until moving to full-time roofing around 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and no need to panic. I'd keep saying it should be slowed. At work I'd say we're fine for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got a good while. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come, and I'd hope the family store lasts that long. Maybe I'd be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married, buy a house, and keep my job. I'd think about my dad's roofing in a few years. I wouldn't change anything yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have kids in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably in a couple of years. Ten years feels like enough to raise them a bit before anything changes. Elena wants two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is waiting a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I've seen lots of big promises come and go, so I'd rather wait than jump too early.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time** and no need to panic.
I'd keep saying it should be **slowed**, while telling colleagues we're fine.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when robots come, and I hope the store lasts.
I might be **wrong**, but I'd rather wait than jump early.
do: Get married, **buy a house** and keep my job.
Think about my dad's **roofing** in a few years.
S4.quote: I've seen lots of big promises come and go, so I'd rather wait than jump too early.
fieldNote: A decade lets him keep his **family plans** unchanged.
He leans on **scepticism** of big promises to justify waiting.
**Roofing** stays a back-up he'd look at later.

steps.text: Keep the till job at the family-owned store
Marry Elena, buy a house and plan for two children
Wait a few years before looking at roofing work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to switch and it hits right around the wedding and the house. What would help is apprenticeships for grown men, paid, not handouts. And family firms getting a fair go against the big chains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. My dad's trade is my back-up plan, and lots of people don't have that. Without family, I don't know what I'd do.

headlineQuote: My dad's trade is my back-up plan, and lots of people don't have that.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** cashier at a family-owned supermarket in his hometown, nine years in.
He has a **year's savings**, a paid-off car and a church wedding planned with Elena.
He never uses **AI** and blames big chains and tech firms for any cuts.
When AGI comes fast, he turns to **family**, especially his dad's roofing trade.
With more time he prefers to **wait**, distrustful of big promises.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits right around his wedding and house purchase.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults, not handouts, and a fair go for family firms.
